profile.summary: CycPepNet compares molecular representations and machine learning models on cyclic peptides for three properties: binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life. Each property is posed twice, as regression on the measured value and as classification against a stated threshold, giving 20 tasks. The framework covers those 20 tasks, 45 model configurations, two split methods and five seeds, and its analyses draw on a main pool of 22 configurations. The data come from six published cyclic peptide sources, which the framework does not redistribute: it ships an inventory with each input file's hash, a curator per source, the released split indices and the full archive of run records, so the published tables and figures can be reproduced without retraining. Its own result table shows the point: test root mean square errors on the small binding sets sit close to the mean baseline, while the larger permeability sets are predictable.

summary_quotes.text: CycPepNet is an open framework that compares molecular representations and machine-learning models for cyclic-peptide **binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life**.

The framework covers 20 regression/classification tasks, 45 model configurations, two split methods and five training seeds. Saved run records allow every analysis and figure to be reproduced without retraining models.
The framework snapshot is nine exact provider files. They are **not distributed with this repository**: acquire each one from its provider under the terms that provider sets.
Analyses draw on a main pool of 22 configurations: the 44 less the higher-radius fingerprints and the PhysChem-augmented variants, which enter only the paired ablations.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How far machine learning can get on cyclic peptides, a class where the data are scarce and scattered. Three properties are covered: binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life. Each is set up as a regression on the measured value and as a classification against a fixed cut, an inhibition constant or half maximal concentration at or below 100 nanomolar for binding, a log permeability at or above minus 6, and a half-life of 8 hours or more. Because the model and representation matrix is held fixed across tasks, the comparison is as much about which molecular representation helps as about which model wins, and the framework's own result table compares each selected model against a mean baseline on the same test split.

quotes.text: CycPepNet is an open framework that compares molecular representations and machine-learning models for cyclic-peptide **binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life**.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Six published sources supply the measurements: CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD for permeability, Macrocycle-DB for binding affinity, and PEPlife2, PepMSND and PepTherDia for half-life. Nine exact provider files make up the snapshot and none of them is redistributed; an inventory records each one's size, hash, acquisition address and identity check, and most carry the status that redistribution terms are not established. Each source has its own curator script, and the permeability and half-life combinations are separate curation steps. One function, load_task_table, applies everything that defines a task: the filters, for example a single target and activity type within Macrocycle-DB, dropping missing values, deduplicating on SMILES by averaging replicate measurements and discarding any molecule whose replicates have a coefficient of variation above 1, the base-10 log transform of the target, and the classification threshold. The released splits are generated with an 80, 10, 10 ratio and a fixed seed, in two flavours: a Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints with a cutoff of 0.45, and a random split. The split size table shows how small the sets are: 28 test molecules for the binding task on one target, 19 for the combined half-life task, against 695 for CycPeptMPDB permeability.

Each source keeps its own curator in `cycpepnet/process/process_<source>.py`; the permeability and half-life combinations are separate scientific steps in `cycpepnet/combine/`.

Task filtering, duplicate handling, log transforms and classification thresholds are centralized in `benchmark.load_task_table`, which needs no fingerprints, so analysis and training apply identical row ordering and target transformations.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model is trained on the train split, its hyper-parameters are chosen on the validation split, with Optuna over 50 trials for every non-baseline configuration, and it is scored on the test split. Selection is on the primary validation metric and reporting is on test, and the README states that nothing is reselected on a companion metric. The primary metric is the root mean square error for the regression tasks and balanced accuracy for the classification tasks, with Q squared F3 and the area under the ROC curve as companions and the coefficient of determination kept as descriptive. Each result is the mean over five seeds, with a seed standard deviation, a seed confidence interval and a separate test-set confidence interval, and the mean baseline's value on the same split. Root mean square error is never pooled across tasks because it carries each task's units; cross-task summaries use ranks, per-task min-max scores or dimensionless metrics, and the released tables include Friedman and Nemenyi ranks and adjusted p values for the confirmatory comparisons.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Two routes. To check and reproduce the published analysis, install the package on Python 3.12 and run three commands: a verification pass that hashes the released artefacts and validates all 40 splits against the task tables they index, a reproduction pass that runs the analysis stages in order and stops at the first failure, and a comparison pass that checks the regenerated tables against the release to a tolerance of 1e-8. The README says these three need neither of the full environments and write 85 CSV and TeX outputs and 17 figures into a separate directory. To train models, install the locked Pixi environment, which is the one the published results came from, generate the fingerprint cache from the released tables, then call the runner with a task, a model, seeds and a split method. To rebuild the data from scratch, the provider files must be acquired first and verified by hash.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Six published sources behind nine provider files: CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD for permeability, Macrocycle-DB for binding affinity, PEPlife2, PepMSND and PepTherDia for half-life. Ten distinct curated data splits, each used for a regression and a classification task, giving 20 tasks. Test set sizes from the released split table: 28 for Macrocycle-DB OPRM1, 49 for MC4R, 32 for SSTR2, 695 for CycPeptMPDB, 109 for NPMMPD, 288 for the CycPeptMPDB Townsend subset, 92 for the NPMMPD Rzepiela subset, 798 for the combined CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD set, and 19 for the combined half-life set.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two released split methods per task, both 80, 10, 10 train, validation and test with seed 42: a Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints at a Tanimoto cutoff of 0.45, and a random split. facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Root mean square error, lower is better, as the primary metric for the regression tasks, with Q squared F3 as its companion, higher is better, and the coefficient of determination as a descriptive extra. Balanced accuracy, higher is better, as the primary metric for the classification tasks, with the area under the ROC curve as its companion. Selection uses the primary validation metric. Root mean square error is never pooled across tasks because it is in each task's own units; cross-task comparison uses ranks or dimensionless metrics.

quotes.text: RMSE is reported in the units of each task's response, so it is never averaged or pooled across tasks: cross-task summaries use ranks, per-task min–max scores or dimensionless metrics.
Any table selecting a configuration selects on the primary validation metric and reports on test; nothing is reselected on a companion metric.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: A mean predictor is the explicit baseline, and the released result table prints its value on the same test split beside each selected model, for example 1.7469 root mean square error against the selected model's 1.4303 on Macrocycle-DB OPRM1 regression, and 0.5 balanced accuracy for the classification tasks. The comparison set is the model and representation matrix itself: random forests and XGBoost on physicochemical descriptors and several fingerprint families, LSTM and transformer models on SMILES and fragSMILES, graph convolutional and message passing networks, two pretrained graph networks and two pretrained chemical language models, with the analyses drawing on a main pool of 22 configurations.

quotes.text: Analyses draw on a main pool of 22 configurations: the 44 less the higher-radius fingerprints and the PhysChem-augmented variants, which enter only the paired ablations.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Three. A Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints at a 0.45 cutoff is released alongside the random split, so a method can be judged on structurally separated molecules. Duplicate structures are collapsed before splitting, by averaging replicate measurements and dropping molecules whose replicates disagree too much. Hyper-parameters are tuned on the validation split only, and the test split is used for reporting, with no reselection on a companion metric. The fingerprint and graph caches carry manifests that refuse a cache whose ordered SMILES or implementation hash do not match.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Five training seeds per configuration, and the released table reports for each task the mean, the standard deviation across seeds, a confidence interval over seeds and a separate confidence interval over the test set, for example a seed interval of 1.3762 to 1.4826 against a test interval of 1.0557 to 1.8049 on the same 28-molecule task. The statistical tests table carries adjusted p values and the multiplicity families behind them, and a separate table records retired inferences and their replacements.

quotes.text: The framework covers 20 regression/classification tasks, 45 model configurations, two split methods and five training seeds.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A cyclic peptide, given as a SMILES string, with one measured property value. Tasks are per molecule and per property, and duplicate structures are merged before splitting, so one row is one unique structure within a task.

quotes.text: Tasks live in [`cycpepnet/benchmark.py`](cycpepnet/benchmark.py); each has a regression (`_reg`) and a classification (`_cls`) form.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Inapplicable in the usual sense: the examples are synthetic cyclic peptides, not sequences from a species. The binding affinity tasks name human targets, OPRM1, MC4R and SSTR2, in their filters and in the split table.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Three kinds of measurement, taken from the published sources: binding affinity as inhibition constants or half maximal inhibitory concentrations, membrane permeability as a log permeability, and half-life in hours. The target values are log transformed where the task says so, and the classification thresholds are applied on the transformed scale, 100 nanomolar for binding, minus 6 for log permeability and 8 hours for half-life.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Framework definition, Input data; cycpepnet/benchmark.py: task definitions

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The molecule, in whichever representation a model family uses. The released matrix covers physicochemical descriptors, several fingerprint families including ECFP, MAP4C, MXFP and HDF, SMILES and fragSMILES strings, and graph objects, and the two pretrained families read graphs and SMILES. No target structure or sequence is given to the model.

quotes.text: | Fingerprints | RF (`rf_*`), XGBoost (`xgb_*`) | PhysChem, ECFP4/6 b/c, MAP4C/6C, MXFP, HDF |

The model × representation matrix is `BENCHMARK_MATRIX` in [`cycpepnet/runner.py`](cycpepnet/runner.py); representations are the `RepType` enum in [`cycpepnet/evaluation.py`](cycpepnet/evaluation.py).

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training per task, with pretrained models fine-tuned in the same loop. Every non-baseline configuration tunes its hyper-parameters with Optuna over 50 trials on the validation split, and the matrix includes two pretrained graph networks and two pretrained chemical language models alongside models trained from scratch. The README also shows how to drop in an external model: load the task table and the released split, train on train, choose on val and score test with the framework's own metric functions.

strengths.text: The reproduction path is built in and checked. One command hashes the released artefacts and validates all 40 splits against the task tables, another regenerates the analysis, and a third compares the regenerated tables against the release to a tolerance of 1e-8, all without a GPU or retraining.

quotes.text: `cycpepnet.verify` hashes the released artifacts and validates all 40 splits against the task tables they index.
`--compare` checks the regenerated CSV/TeX outputs against the release within `rtol=atol=1e-8`
The analysis stages read the reference run records, curated CSVs and released splits; no GPU, pretrained weights or fingerprint caches are required.

strengths.text: Both a structural and a random split are released for every task, with the clustering parameters in the code, so the gap between them can be read directly rather than argued about.

The reporting discipline is unusually explicit: selection on the primary validation metric with no reselection on a companion, no pooling of root mean square error across tasks, and both seed-level and test-level confidence intervals in the released table.

quotes.text: Any table selecting a configuration selects on the primary validation metric and reports on test; nothing is reselected on a companion metric.
RMSE is reported in the units of each task's response, so it is never averaged or pooled across tasks: cross-task summaries use ranks, per-task min–max scores or dimensionless metrics.

strengths.text: The data provenance is documented rather than assumed. An inventory records every input file with its hash, acquisition address and reviewed licence status, a separate evidence file holds the review, and the README states plainly that verification establishes identity, not redistribution rights.

quotes.text: [`data/sources.csv`](data/sources.csv) records each one with its SHA-256 hash, acquisition link and review status
This establishes file identity, not redistribution rights.

limitations.text: The test sets are tiny for most tasks. The released split table gives 19 test molecules for the combined half-life task and 28, 32 and 49 for the three binding tasks, and the released result table shows test confidence intervals far wider than the seed intervals, for example 1.0557 to 1.8049 against 1.3762 to 1.4826.

The input data cannot simply be downloaded. Nine provider files are needed and none is redistributed; the inventory marks most as having redistribution terms not established, and the README records specific unresolved problems: the NPMMPD snapshot differs from the Figshare version, the PEPlife2 export query has to be recovered, and the PepTherDia selection predicate, scraper and page order have not been recovered.

run_guide.summary: Verify the released artefacts, regenerate the published analysis and compare it against the release.
prerequisites: Python 3.12. For the three analysis commands the README says pip install -e . is enough and no GPU, pretrained weights or fingerprint caches are needed.

For training or curation, the Pixi environment with its exact lockfile, which is where the published results were produced; Conda is offered as an alternative without an exact lock, and Windows is covered by neither.
The code is MIT licensed and does not cover the third-party data. Training from the provider inputs requires acquiring those nine files under their own terms.

steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/molML/CycPepNet.git
cd CycPepNet

steps.title: Verify, reproduce and compare
steps.shell:
python -m cycpepnet.verify
python -m cycpepnet.reproduce
python -m cycpepnet.verify --compare outputs/reproduction/results
steps.explanation: The README's three reproduction commands, written without the pixi run prefix because it states these three work under a plain pip install. The first hashes the released artefacts and validates all 40 splits, the second runs the analysis stages in order and stops at the first failure, and the third compares the regenerated outputs against the release to a tolerance of 1e-8.

quotes.text:
pixi run python -m cycpepnet.verify
pixi run python -m cycpepnet.reproduce
pixi run python -m cycpepnet.verify --compare outputs/reproduction/results
`cycpepnet.reproduce` runs the analysis stages in order, stops on the first failure and writes a `reproduction.json` marker only if every stage succeeds.

steps.title: Train one model on one task
steps.shell:
pixi run python -m cycpepnet.prepare --dataset macrocycledb --stage representations \
  --from-release --representations morgan_fp
pixi run python -m cycpepnet.runner --tasks macrocycledb_mc4r_ki_reg --models mean \
  --seeds 0 --split-method butina_morgan --data-root outputs/processed
steps.explanation: The README's example: generate the fingerprint cache from the released tables, then run the runner for one task, one model, one seed and the Butina split. These commands need the full environment.
